titolo: Dario Amodei's Anthropic: Did Claude Just Crack the Riemann Hypothesis?
angolo: A mathematician at Dario Amodei's freshly listed company claims Claude helped prove math's biggest problem, minutes after a record IPO, and the world now has to check if it is true.
descrizione: Dario Amodei's Anthropic: did Claude just crack the Riemann hypothesis? A mathematician at Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, says he and Claude found a proof of the 167-year-old problem, one day after the company's record Nasdaq debut. It is a claim, not a verified result: the Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the problem as unsolved, and a rival human-written draft from Stanford appeared the same day. Here is what is confirmed, what is only reported, and what happens next.

scene.testo: A mathematician at Anthropic claims an AI helped him solve math's greatest riddle.
The riddle is 167 years old, counting from 1859.
He says he found the proof working with Claude, Anthropic's AI.
The question: is it true, and what happens to Dario Amodei's company if it is?

grafica.sotto: Anthropic's claim about the Riemann hypothesis

scene.testo: This is the Riemann hypothesis, posed in 1859.
It concerns how prime numbers are spread across infinity.
Primes are numbers divisible only by one and themselves.
Many call it the Holy Grail of mathematics.
It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems.
The Clay Mathematics Institute offers one million dollars for a solution.
But hours after the announcement, the Clay Institute still listed the problem as unsolved.
Why? Because the proof comes as millions of lines of computer code that mathematicians have yet to understand.
In a moment: the 17-million-line problem nobody can read.
First, who is behind it.
His name is Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic.
He is described as a member of the company's technical staff.
He says the discovery came late on a Sunday night, November 15.
He says he then messaged the company's chief executive, Dario Amodei.
He asked about his ability to announce it, according to NPR.
This is Dario Amodei, Anthropic's chief executive.
His company was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees.
Back in August, Anthropic had published research on a related result.
An unreleased Claude model improved a long-standing result related to the hypothesis, Anthropic said.
Anthropic said plainly that it was not a full proof.
Three months later, Alpöge says he went all the way.
On Friday, November 20, he posted a four-page note on his website.
His central sentence is short and careful.
Note the words: I believe. He is claiming, not declaring victory.
He says the method also covers the generalized Riemann hypothesis.
That is a broader version, covering a whole family of functions.
He did not publish a conventional paper.
He released the argument in Lean, a proof-checking programming language.
Lean checks reasoning step by step, line by line.
NPR puts the size at 17 million lines of Lean code.
A written version would have run past 250,000 pages, according to Alpöge's note as reported by AFP and the BBC.
He was open about who did the heavy lifting.
Claude, he wrote, far outpaced him near the finish line.
There is one more detail. The timing.
The day before, Anthropic had rung the Nasdaq opening bell.
It was Thursday, November 19, in New York.
The company raised a record 81.3 billion dollars at the offering.
If underwriters exercise their option to buy more shares, the total would rise to about 93.5 billion dollars.
The IPO price valued the company at about 1.5 trillion dollars, including employee options and restricted shares.
Shares closed 17 percent higher, on a day the Nasdaq fell over two percent.
In a speech at the Nasdaq, Dario Amodei spoke about doing the right thing.
A day later, his own mathematician made the claim.
According to AFP, Alpöge acknowledged the timing could be viewed cynically, without elaborating.
He said he consulted Amodei before announcing, per the same AFP report.
Now to the question that matters: will the proof survive?
Because within hours, a second claim appeared, with no AI involved.
Stanford professor Ravi Vakil posted a draft proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis by Alessandro Masullo.
Vakil is president of the American Mathematical Society.
The draft is by Alessandro Masullo, who received his Stanford PhD in 2020, according to Nature.
Vakil called it all human, with no AI, TechCrunch reported.
Masullo says it reflects twelve years of work.
It is not in Lean, and it has not been checked, according to TechCrunch.
Two claims in one day. Neither confirmed as settled.

visivo.testo: Two claims in one day. Neither confirmed as settled.

scene.testo: So what do outside experts actually say?
Kevin Buzzard of Imperial College London spoke to New Scientist.
Brian Conrey, a leading specialist, told AFP what the stakes are.
He told AFP: 'It's really the biggest thing I think that's ever happened in mathematics.'
Mathematician Alex Kontorovich told NPR he felt an out-of-body experience.
The Clay Institute's president, Martin Bridson, said a lot of work lay ahead to fully understand the finding.
Scientific American reports that MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland independently compiled the Lean code.
That checks the code. It is not the same as understanding the idea.
So what is confirmed, and what is only reported?
Confirmed: Alpöge published a claimed proof, reported by NPR and AFP.
Not confirmed: that the Riemann hypothesis is solved.
AFP says the claim has not been independently verified and the proof has not been reviewed by outside experts.
This is the second such claim in recent months.
And what does the money say? Anthropic opened at 111.50 dollars.
By Friday's close it was at 88.91, according to CNBC.
Anthropic has not issued a statement on the proof, according to one report.
What happens next? Experts point to slow, careful checking.
If it holds, a Millennium problem falls to a machine. If not, it joins a long list.
For now, it is a claim. The story is still moving.
